clinicalPearls: Subacute, severe, symmetrical proximal weakness with markedly elevated creatine kinase, typically higher than in dermatomyositis or polymyositis.
Two defining myositis-specific antibodies: anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR; a seronegative subgroup also exists.
Anti-HMGCR disease is associated with prior statin exposure, but occurs without statins, particularly in younger patients, and weakness progresses despite drug withdrawal.
Persistence or progression of weakness after stopping a statin distinguishes immune-mediated necrotising myopathy from self-limited toxic statin myopathy.

Muscle biopsy shows scattered necrotic and regenerating fibres with sparse inflammatory infiltrate, sarcolemmal MHC-I upregulation and membrane-attack-complex deposition on capillaries and non-necrotic fibres.
Anti-SRP disease tends to be more severe, treatment-resistant and may involve the myocardium; anti-HMGCR disease often responds well to intravenous immunoglobulin.
Dysphagia is common and an early marker of disease severity.
An underlying occult malignancy should be considered, particularly in older and seronegative patients.
reference.pathophysiology: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy is a humorally driven idiopathic inflammatory myopathy in which antibodies, rather than a T-cell-rich infiltrate, are thought to be directly pathogenic. Circulating anti-signal-recognition-particle (anti-SRP) and anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme-A-reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibodies target antigens expressed on the myofibre surface, with antibody titres broadly tracking disease activity. Complement is activated on the sarcolemma and capillaries, generating membrane-attack complex and leading to repeated cycles of myofibre necrosis and regeneration. Because regenerating fibres re-express HMGCR, which is upregulated by statins, statin exposure is thought to prime and sustain the anti-HMGCR response in genetically susceptible individuals, so autoimmunity continues even after the drug is withdrawn.
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase and other muscle enzymes
Myositis-specific antibody panel including anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR
Electromyography looking for an irritable myopathic pattern
Muscle MRI to detect oedema and guide biopsy site
Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for MHC-I and complement (C5b-9) deposition
Cardiac assessment with echocardiography or cardiac MRI, especially in anti-SRP disease
Age-appropriate malignancy screening and swallow assessment
redFlags: Respiratory muscle weakness and falling respiratory reserve
Cardiac involvement, particularly in anti-SRP disease
reference.prognosis: The course is typically chronic and frequently treatment-refractory, especially with anti-SRP antibodies, requiring prolonged combination immunotherapy and carrying a high relapse rate on tapering. Anti-HMGCR disease often responds well to intravenous immunoglobulin, whereas untreated disease may lead to fixed proximal weakness and disability.
pitfalls: Misattributing persistent weakness to self-limited statin myopathy when it is in fact anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy.
Interpreting the sparse inflammatory infiltrate on biopsy as a muscular dystrophy and overlooking complement and MHC-I markers.
Failing to recognise the seronegative subgroup when standard antibody testing is negative.
Omitting cardiac assessment and malignancy screening.
Undertreating anti-SRP disease, which typically needs early aggressive immunosuppression.
references: European Neuromuscular Centre (ENMC) criteria for immune-mediated necrotising myopathy
EULAR/ACR classification criteria for idiopathic inflammatory myopathies
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Immediate withdrawal of any implicated statin in anti-HMGCR disease, recognising that weakness commonly progresses despite cessation and still requires immunotherapy
Corticosteroids as initial immunosuppression, with early introduction of a steroid-sparing agent such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil
Intravenous immunoglobulin, which is particularly effective in anti-HMGCR disease and may be used as an early or sole agent
Rituximab or other escalation for anti-SRP or treatment-refractory disease
Physiotherapy and graded rehabilitation to preserve muscle strength and function
Monitoring of creatine kinase, antibody titres and objective muscle strength to track disease activity and guide tapering
Cardiac surveillance with echocardiography or cardiac MRI, especially in anti-SRP disease which may involve the myocardium
Management within a combined rheumatology and neuromuscular service
